text: A great deal of tabular analysis follows one pattern: split the rows into groups defined by some key column, apply a summary to each group, and combine the summaries back into a single table or mapping. The split key is usually a categorical column; the summary is a reduction such as a count, a sum, or an average. Thinking in this split-apply-combine shape, rather than writing explicit loops, keeps the intent clear and the code vectorized.

Once rows are grouped, you choose a reduction that answers your question. A count tells you how many rows fall in each group; a sum totals a numeric column; an average (the arithmetic mean) describes a typical value per group. Picking the right reduction is a modeling choice, not a mechanical one: an average hides spread, so pair it with a measure of variation when the groups differ in size or skew.

Tidy data puts one observation per row and one variable per column, which is what makes grouping and aggregation straightforward. When you read a CSV, check the column names, the data types, and whether a header row was parsed correctly before doing anything else. Most wrangling bugs trace back to a column read as text when you expected a number, or a stray index column.

tags: Fitting a line by least squares
text: Linear regression assumes the target is approximately a weighted sum of the inputs plus an intercept. Least squares chooses the weights that minimize the total squared error between predictions and observed targets on the training data. Adding an intercept term (a constant feature) lets the line sit away from the origin. The fitted weights are interpretable: each one is the change in the prediction per unit change in its input, holding the others fixed.

A model that is only scored on the data it was fit to will look better than it is. Held-out evaluation keeps a separate test split that the model never sees during fitting, and reports a metric there. For regression, the coefficient of determination (R-squared) summarizes how much of the target's variation the model explains on that unseen split; values near one are strong, values near zero mean the model barely beats predicting the average.

Leakage is any way information from the test split sneaks into fitting, making held-out scores optimistic and the model worse in the wild. Common forms: fitting a scaler or imputer on the full dataset before splitting, choosing features by looking at the test labels, or tuning until the test score is high. The discipline is simple to state and easy to violate: decide the split first, then treat the test split as if it does not exist until the very end.

A perceptron computes a weighted sum of its inputs and passes it through a nonlinear activation function. Stacking a layer of these units (the hidden layer) in front of an output unit gives a multilayer perceptron, which can represent curved decision boundaries that a single linear unit cannot. The hidden width is a capacity knob: too few units underfit, too many can overfit a small dataset.

tags: Training loss and the learning rate
text: Training minimizes a loss that measures how far predictions are from targets; for regression-style outputs the mean squared error is common. The learning rate scales each update: too large and the loss bounces or diverges, too small and training crawls. Watch the loss curve over iterations rather than a single number, and seed your random initialization so a run is reproducible.

Optimization here is local search on a loss surface: from the current weights, take a small step in the direction that most reduces the loss, then repeat. Because the surface is not convex for these networks, where you start and how big your steps are both matter, and you may settle in different basins on different seeds. Convergence is a property to check empirically, by watching the loss flatten, not to assume.

Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's running time or memory grows as the input size grows, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. Linear time means the work grows in proportion to the input; quadratic time means it grows with the square of the input, which becomes painful quickly. The point is to compare how approaches scale, not to predict exact milliseconds.

A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece of the same problem until it reaches a base case that can be answered directly. The two things to get right are the base case, so the recursion stops, and the step that makes the subproblem strictly smaller, so it makes progress toward the base case. Without both, recursion either never stops or never simplifies.

Choosing a data structure is choosing which operations are cheap. A list keeps order and is cheap to append to, but searching it scans every element. A hash map gives near-constant-time lookup by key but does not preserve order. Picking the structure that makes your most frequent operation cheap usually matters more than micro-optimizing the code around a poor choice.

A good unit test pins one behavior: given a specific input, the code produces a specific output, and the test fails loudly if that changes. Tests are most useful when they are deterministic and hermetic, depending on no network, clock, or hidden state, so a failure means the behavior changed and not that the environment did. Write the test you wish had caught the last bug.
